title: A small group
hookLine: a few people who know how your soul is
tomorrow: why would someone skip lunch on a Wednesday on purpose?

lines: THE REAL ANSWER GOES TO A FEW.
cards: How are you? Fine, thanks. That's the version for the office and the checkout line.
The real answer, the one about your soul, usually goes to very few people: the ones who'd notice if you went quiet. Take a rope in your hands for a second, even in your mind. One strand snaps easily.
Twist three together and it holds a weight. An old book in the Bible uses exactly that picture, and it starts with someone falling down.

teach.h: IF THEY FALL, ONE LIFTS THE OTHER.
teach.b: Ecclesiastes, in the King James Bible: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
A few lines later comes the rope: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” A small group is a few strands twisted together, people who notice when you fall.

teach.h: TWO OR THREE, IN MY NAME.
teach.b: Jesus puts a number on how small a gathering can be: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” Two or three. A kitchen table is enough.
No stage, no program, no sign-up sheet. And here's the detail to tell a friend: that promise sits in a passage about what to do when someone has wronged you. The small circle isn't only for comfort.
It's where the hard conversations happen too. The letters show the rest.
Paul: “Bear ye one another's burdens.” James: “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed.”
Churches call these circles different things, a house group, a Bible study, a prayer partner, breakfast with the same friends. The strands change. The cord holds.

how: Some Christians meet weekly in a small group, often called a house group, cell group or Bible study, to read scripture, share honestly and pray for one another; others keep one or two prayer partners.

o: a few people who know how your soul is doing
a church committee that plans the weekly events
a class for new members before they can join

games.q: the strands of the cord — tap the pairs.
p: two or three, in my name
confess your faults one to another

s: "two or three gathered" is a promise only for big church meetings
the number Jesus gives is small: where two or three are gathered together in my name.
Matthew's "two or three" line sits in a passage about settling a wrong
it follows teaching on what to do when someone trespasses against you.
Ecclesiastes says a threefold cord is not quickly broken
a few lines after two are better than one.

games.q: you start college in a new city and know nobody. a huge campus ministry meets weekly; a dorm Bible study has four people. you can only do one. what does today's lesson point you toward?
o: the four: a few who'd notice if you fell.
the huge one: more people means more support.
neither for now: faith is private until you settle in.
games.why: Ecclesiastes wants someone to lift you when you fall, and Jesus' promise needs only two or three. a big room can be good too; the lesson is about the few who know you.

practice: Hold your phone in one hand and count on the other the two or three people who'd get your real answer. If the count comes up short, that's worth knowing too.
Then send one of them a message that asks how they actually are, and means it.

wordCard.voice: A small group. A few strands twisted into one cord: people who lift you when you fall, and a promise that needs only two or three.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: two or three, a cord not quickly broken, even when one strand frays. Talk tomorrow.
